item.title: Strategic Brief: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns and Faces a Congressional Probe, Chris Van Hollen Challenges Chuck Schumer for Senate Leader, and Trump Pulls JD Vance Off Iran Talks
item.description:
Nvidia names CFO Colette Kress interim CEO after Jensen Huang steps down and agrees to testify alongside Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick; Sen. Chris Van Hollen challenges Chuck Schumer after Democratic midterm gains; Trump halts Vance's Iran diplomacy and floats military action against Cuba; and Finland detects a strike on a Russian warship.
► Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Espionage Probe and Agrees to Testify Before Congress According to BBC, The Guardian, and CNBC, Nvidia co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after revelations of extramarital relationships involving two company subordinates and an intermediary—identified by Le Monde as Alice H Why it matters: Huang's sudden exit and the joint congressional summons of Nvidia's founder and the US Commerce Secretary turn a corporate governance scandal into a national-security investigation over US-China semiconductor export controls.
► Chris Van Hollen Challenges Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader After Midterm Sweep According to The Guardian and AP News, Maryland Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen announced on Thursday that he will challenge veteran New York Senator Chuck Schumer for the post of US Senate Majority Leader in the incoming 120th Congress. Why it matters: Van Hollen's rare leadership challenge against Schumer signals deep generational and foreign-policy restlessness inside the enlarged Senate Democratic caucus.
► Trump Orders Vance to Drop Iran Ceasefire Talks and Hints at Military Action Against Cuba According to AP News and The Independent, US President Donald Trump ordered Vice President JD Vance to abandon backchannel ceasefire negotiations with Tehran and redirect his focus toward investigating alleged domestic corruption and fraud in Democra Why it matters: Sidelining Vance from Iran diplomacy while floating military intervention in Cuba and tariff hikes on Mexico shows the White House pivoting toward unilateral pressure after its midterm losses.
► Finland Detects Strike on Russian Warship in Baltic Sea as Putin Agrees to European Talks Role According to Al Jazeera and Defense News, Finland's military announced on Thursday that it detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, though Helsinki added that regional maritime security remains stable. Why it matters: Bringing European capitals into the next negotiating round closes a major rift between Washington and Brussels, even as Baltic naval strikes and Starshield disruptions underscore active battlefield pressure.
► Federal Reserve Drops Rate Vote From October 2027 Meeting as Yen Breaches 160 According to CNBC and The Wall Street Journal, the US Federal Reserve announced a policy calendar switch under which its October 26–27, 2027 Federal Open Market Committee meeting will be dedicated to long-term framework deliberation without a formal Why it matters: A $404. 1 billion single-month US fiscal deficit and rising Treasury yields are driving the dollar above 160 yen and straining emerging-market trade balances.
■ The Bottom Line Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia and congressional subpoenas for both Huang and Commerce Secretary Lutnick rattle the AI sector, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen's challenge to Chuck Schumer and Trump's halt to Vance's Iran talks reshape Washington's post-midterm power struggle.

item.title: Strategic Brief: US Envoys Head to Moscow and Dublin After Abu Dhabi Talks, Scott Colom Flips Mississippi's Senate Seat, and Indonesia's Vice President Resigns
item.description:
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner carry ceasefire proposals from Abu Dhabi to Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy; Democrat Scott Colom becomes Mississippi's first Black US senator since Reconstruction; Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka steps down over a degree dispute; and Pope Leo XIV returns to Peru.
► US Envoys Carry Abu Dhabi Proposals to Putin in Moscow and Zelenskyy in Dublin According to France 24, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and to Dublin to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, building on two days of trilateral discussions Why it matters: Shuttle diplomacy between Moscow and Dublin tests whether the Abu Dhabi channel can produce a durable freeze or whether local ceasefires like Oleshky simply allow Russian units to stage fresh assaults.
► Democrat Scott Colom Wins Mississippi Senate Race in Historic Upset Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's US Senate race, The Guardian, BBC, and AP News reported after the contest was called eight days past midterm election day. Why it matters: Colom's upset expands Democratic margins in Congress just as the White House braces for subpoena battles over Iran war powers and executive branch oversight.
► Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka Resigns Over Education Row Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka—the eldest son of former President Joko Widodo—resigned on Wednesday following a protracted controversy over the validity of his educational qualifications, Al Jazeera reported. Why it matters: Gibran's sudden departure upends President Prabowo Subianto's ruling coalition in Jakarta, while Taipei's choice of chip and PC pioneer Stan Shih for Shenzhen puts cross-strait protocol to an immediate test.
► Pope Leo XIV Returns to Peru as European States Push UN Action on West Bank Pope Leo XIV—the first American-born pontiff, who spent two decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship—returned to Lima to mammoth crowds, The New York Times and The Washington Post reported. Why it matters: European moves to sanction settler officials at border controls and convene the UN Security Council over E1 mark a sharper break with Israeli settlement policy.
► General Strike Draws 120,000 in Madrid as Brooklyn Building Collapse Kills Two Approximately 120,000 protesters marched through rain in Madrid during Spain's first general strike since 2012, Euronews reported, rallying against soaring housing costs and household budget pressures, while clashes broke out between riot police and Why it matters: Spain's mass housing walkout underscores mounting cost-of-living anger across Western Europe, while Bessent's move onto a military base shows Iranian retaliation threats reaching top US economic officials.
■ The Bottom Line US envoys carry Abu Dhabi truce proposals to Moscow and Dublin even as Kyiv warns the Oleshky ceasefire is aiding Russian river crossings, while Democrat Scott Colom's historic Mississippi Senate win and Indonesian Vice President Gibran's resignation reshape domestic coalitions.

item.title: Strategic Brief: The US House Blocks Pete Hegseth's Impeachment 211-204, Gadi Eisenkot Pushes an October 7 Inquiry as Israel's New Knesset Convenes, and DR Congo's Ebola Death Toll Passes 5,300
item.description:
House Republicans voted 211-204 to refer eight impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee even as a Reuters/Ipsos poll showed 71 percent of Americans want Congress to end the Iran war; Israel's opposition-led Knesset was sworn in with coalition formateur Gadi Eisenkot introducing legislation for a state inquiry into the October 7 attacks; and health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo reported that the country's largest Ebola outbreak has exceeded 11,000 cases and 5,387 deaths.
► House Blocks Hegseth Impeachment 211-204 as Bessent Relocates Over Iran Threats The Republican-controlled US House of Representatives voted 211-204 late Tuesday to refer Representative Thomas Massie's eight-article impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee, stalling the remova Why it matters: Referring Hegseth's impeachment resolution to committee by a seven-vote margin only postpones the confrontation until January, when a new Democratic majority takes the gavel backed by 71 percent public support for ending the Iran conflict.
► Israel's New Knesset Convenes With Oct. 7 Inquiry Push as US Senators Challenge NDAA Clauses Dozens of newly elected lawmakers were sworn into Israel's parliament on Tuesday as the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot assumed a parliamentary majority following the October 27 election (New York Times, DW). Why it matters: With an opposition majority now seated in the Knesset, Eisenkot can pass a statutory October 7 inquiry into Netanyahu's conduct by simple majority even before completing formal coalition talks.
► Abu Dhabi Talks Enter Day Two as Zelensky Signals Readiness to Discuss Territory Delegations from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States opened a second day of trilateral ceasefire negotiations in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday after Washington proposed a new European security arrangement on day one (France 24, AFP). Why it matters: Zelensky's explicit statement that Kyiv is ready to discuss territorial issues marks a major rhetorical shift aimed at keeping Washington aligned with Ukraine during the Abu Dhabi negotiations.
► DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Passes 5,300 Deaths and South Korea Fines Bond Dealers 1.6T Won Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo reported that the country's worst-ever Ebola epidemic has surpassed 11,000 confirmed and probable cases with at least 5,387 deaths, as ongoing militia fighting in the eastern provinces and de Why it matters: An Ebola outbreak exceeding 11,000 cases and 5,387 deaths in conflict-hit eastern Congo risks cross-border transmission into neighboring Great Lakes states unless international medical access is secured.
■ The Bottom Line Overnight developments underscored deep political and security transitions from Washington to Jerusalem and Abu Dhabi: House Republicans voted 211-204 to refer Pete Hegseth's impeachment resolution to committee even as 71 percent of Americans polled backed ending the Iran war and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base over Iranian threats. In Jerusalem, an opposition majority took control of the Knesset as Gadi Eisenkot pushed an October 7 state inquiry, while in Abu Dhabi, Ukraine and Russia entered a second day of US-mediated talks with President Zelensky signaling readiness to discuss territorial questions. Meanwhile, DR Congo's Ebola outbreak passed 11,000 cases and 5,387 deaths, UK police arrested a US soldier suspected of spying for Russia, and South Korea fined 15 bond dealers 1.6 trillion won for collusion.

item.title: Strategic Brief: China's October Exports Surge 35.2%, Washington Floats Article 5-Style Guarantees Ahead of Abu Dhabi Ukraine Talks, and Rubio Says Israel No Longer Needs US Financial Aid
item.description:
China's outbound shipments jumped 35.2 percent year-on-year in October while strong import growth narrowed its monthly trade surplus; US, Russian, and Ukrainian negotiators are set to convene in Abu Dhabi as Washington proposes NATO Article 4 and 5-style security guarantees for Kyiv; and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared after G7 talks in Paris that Israel can purchase American weapons without further US financial assistance.
► China's October Trade Surge and Asia-Pacific Monetary Shifts Customs data released Tuesday showed China's dollar-denominated exports expanded 35. 2 percent year-on-year in October, outpacing market expectations of 33. Why it matters: China's 35. 2 percent export surge alongside a narrower trade surplus shows how war-inflated raw material import prices are offsetting stronger factory export volumes across East Asia.
► Abu Dhabi Trilateral Ukraine Talks and European Security Commitments Negotiators from Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv are scheduled to hold trilateral discussions in Abu Dhabi as the White House tests a ceasefire formula built around binding Western security commitments (NTV, Yeni Şafak). Why it matters: Offering Kyiv Article 5-style mutual defense commitments outside formal NATO accession is Washington's clearest attempt yet to bridge Ukraine's security demands with Moscow's red line on alliance enlargement.
► Rubio's Israel Aid Remarks, Gaza Stabilization Force, and Gulf Diplomacy Speaking after G7 foreign ministers' talks in Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio signaled a shift in bilateral defense financing by stating that Israel can continue purchasing US military hardware using its own budget but no longer needs Americ Why it matters: Rubio's statement that Israel no longer requires US financial grant aid reflects growing fiscal and political pressure in Washington to transition Israel from military grants to cash-only foreign military sales.
► US Post-Midterm Clash Over War Powers and the Antalya COP31 Summit In Washington, Republican Representative Thomas Massie filed an eight-article impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of executing unauthorized combat strikes in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela and citing Why it matters: Massie's eight-article impeachment resolution against Hegseth brings bipartisan congressional scrutiny over unauthorized strikes in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela directly onto the House floor ahead of the new legislative term.
■ The Bottom Line Tuesday brought simultaneous diplomatic maneuvering and trade surprises: China's October exports jumped 35.2 percent year-on-year even as surging commodity import costs narrowed its trade surplus, while US, Russian, and Ukrainian envoys prepared to meet in Abu Dhabi over a US proposal for NATO Article 5-style security guarantees for Kyiv. In the Middle East, Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared after G7 talks in Paris that Israel no longer needs US financial aid to buy American arms, President Trump cited 'positive momentum' toward ending the Iran conflict after meeting Qatar's prime minister, Republican Rep. Thomas Massie filed eight impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and 95 world leaders gathered in Antalya for the COP31 climate summit.

item.title: Strategic Brief: A Drone Strike on Iraq's Khor Mor Field Cuts 70% of Kurdish Power, China's Producer Inflation Hits 5.7%, and Egypt Reopens Its Tripoli Embassy After 12 Years
item.description:
An unmanned aerial strike forced a production halt at northern Iraq's Khor Mor gas facility and knocked out electricity across more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region, even as oil futures eased after President Trump said fresh US strikes on Iran were unlikely. Elsewhere, China's October producer price index jumped 5.7 percent to a four-year high on rising energy input costs while consumer inflation cooled, Cairo reopened its embassy in Tripoli after a 12-year closure, and G7 foreign ministers convened in Paris to press Washington on Ukraine and Iran.
► Drone Strike Halts Iraq's Khor Mor Gas Field as Trump Calls Fresh Iran Strikes 'Unlikely' An explosive drone struck the Khor Mor gas facility in Iraq's Sulaymaniyah province late Sunday, halting gas production and triggering widespread blackouts that left more than 70 percent of northern Iraq's Kurdish region without electricity (Al Jazee Why it matters: Even as the White House cools talk of new direct strikes on Iran after midterm losses, the Khor Mor blackout shows militia drone attacks on Iraqi energy infrastructure remain an active pressure point outside formal US-Iran talks.
► Post-Midterm Reckoning in Washington as G7 Ministers Meet in Paris Reflecting on Tuesday's Republican midterm defeat in a Sunday interview with CBS's '60 Minutes,' President Donald Trump acknowledged that his administration's deportation policies had been 'too tough' and hurt Republicans at the ballot box, stating h Why it matters: Trump's public admission on '60 Minutes' that immigration enforcement and the Iran war cost Republicans Congress signals a tactical pivot toward deal-making ahead of January's power transfer on Capitol Hill.
► China's Producer Inflation Surges 5.7% to Four-Year High While Consumer Demand Cools China's National Bureau of Statistics reported on Monday that the country's producer price index (PPI) rose 5. 7 percent year-on-year in October — the highest reading in more than four years and above the 5. Why it matters: A 5. 7 percent factory-gate inflation print paired with soft consumer prices squeezes Chinese industrial profit margins: manufacturers are paying war-inflated energy costs without being able to pass them on to domestic shoppers.
► Egypt Reopens Tripoli Embassy After 12 Years as Gaza Landslide Kills Five Egypt formally reopened its embassy in Tripoli, Libya, over the weekend, restoring diplomatic representation in the Libyan capital for the first time since violence forced the mission's closure in 2014 (Yeni Şafak). Why it matters: Cairo's return to Tripoli after 12 years of backing rival eastern Libyan factions marks a major diplomatic realignment in North Africa, giving Egypt direct leverage in the UN-recognized capital alongside Turkey.
► Antalya Hosts 196 Nations for COP31 as Pope Leo XIV Rebukes Milei's Austerity in Argentina Delegations from 196 countries convened in Antalya, Turkey, on Monday for the opening of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), the first time Turkey has hosted the flagship global climate summit (Anadolu Agency, Yeni Şafak). Why it matters: As COP31 opens in Antalya, the gap between $305 billion in needed adaptation funds and under $32 billion in actual disbursements makes climate finance — rather than new emissions targets — the summit's central fault line.
■ The Bottom Line Monday opened with conflicting signals across the Middle East energy and security landscape: oil prices dipped after President Trump said fresh US strikes on Iran were 'unlikely,' yet an overnight drone attack halted northern Iraq's Khor Mor gas field and cut electricity to more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region as CENTCOM activated its 'Iron Gate' land-interdiction task force. In Washington, Trump acknowledged on '60 Minutes' that tough deportations and the Iran war hurt Republicans in the midterms, offering Democrats an immigration deal...

item.title: Strategic Brief: Washington Launches a Task Force Against Iran's Land Routes, Saudi Arabia Sounds Civil Defense Alerts in Dhahran, and New Zealand's Election Ends on a Knife-Edge
item.description:
US forces widened the eight-month Iran blockade from sea to land by establishing a ground-supply interdiction task force and firing on a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman, even as Saudi civil defense sirens sounded across Dhahran, Dammam, and Abqaiq during Houthi clashes. In the Pacific, New Zealand's general election left parliament separated by a single provisional seat ahead of special vote counts, while Spain's Canary Island of El Hierro declared a state of emergency after 3,300 boat arrivals in the first week of November.
► US Expands Iran Blockade to Land Routes and Fires on Cargo Vessel in Gulf of Oman The United States military announced on Saturday night that it has established a new task force dedicated to disrupting Iran's land-based supply routes used to transport weapons and military materiel across the region, expanding what had previously o Why it matters: Pairing a naval blockade with a dedicated land-corridor interdiction task force stretches US surveillance and strike commitments across Iraq and Syria at the exact moment Tehran removes its missile range cap.
► Saudi Arabia Activates Warning Sirens Across Eastern Oil Hub Amid Houthi Clashes Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense Directorate activated emergency warning sirens across multiple areas of the kingdom's oil-producing Eastern Province — including Dammam, Al-Ahsa, Abqaiq, and Dhahran, home to Saudi Aramco's headquarters — amid ongoing cla Why it matters: Warning sirens in Dhahran and Abqaiq underscore that Saudi energy infrastructure remains under direct aerial threat despite intensive ground operations inside Yemen.
► New Zealand Faces Weeks of Coalition Uncertainty After Knife-Edge Vote New Zealand's general election ended without a clear governing mandate on Saturday night, leaving the country facing weeks of coalition talks while electoral authorities count special and overseas ballots (The Guardian, Times of Israel). Why it matters: Until special ballots are counted, Wellington cannot finalize a coalition agreement, prolonging policy uncertainty over fiscal spending and defense commitments in the South Pacific.
► Poland Declares National Mourning After Kraków Attack as Canary Islands Declare Emergency Polish President Karol Nawrocki declared two days of national mourning and Prime Minister Donald Tusk labeled Saturday's mass shooting in Kraków an 'act of terrorism' after a gunman dressed in military fatigues opened fire from a car in the city's Ma Why it matters: The discovery of three more victims at the Kraków shooter's home deepens Poland's worst domestic terror investigation in years, while November boat arrivals on El Hierro show Atlantic migration routes accelerating into winter.
► Drone Attack Kills Three Colombian Soldiers as Ukraine Endures Overnight Strikes At least three Colombian soldiers were killed and eight seriously injured in an explosive drone attack on a military base, the Colombian army announced, with additional personnel receiving hospital treatment (AP News, Anadolu Agency). Why it matters: Armed groups in Colombia are using multi-casualty drone strikes against regular army bases even as US forces train alongside Colombian units on the ground.
■ The Bottom Line Washington widened its campaign against Tehran this weekend by launching a dedicated task force to interdict Iranian land supply corridors while disabling a blockade-running cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. Across the Gulf, Saudi Arabia briefly activated civil defense sirens in Dhahran, Dammam, and Abqaiq amid Houthi clashes, and Iran declared an end to its self-imposed cap on ballistic missile ranges. item.title: Strategic Brief: Herzog Tasks Eisenkot With Forming Israel's Next Government, a Gunman Kills Six in Kraków, and Paraguay Charges Ex-President Peña Over a Banking Collapse
item.description:
Ten days after Israel's inconclusive October 27 election, President Isaac Herzog handed the coalition mandate to former military chief Gadi Eisenkot with the backing of 67 Knesset members, putting Benjamin Netanyahu closer to the opposition benches than at any point in recent years. In Europe, a far-right-linked shooting in central Kraków killed six people as France faced another weekend of cost-of-living clashes and foreign-linked aviation bomb threats, while in South America a systemic banking failure brought criminal charges against Paraguay's ousted president.

► Six Killed in Kraków Attack as European Security Pressures Mount At least six people — four women and two men — were killed and around 15 others injured on Saturday afternoon when a gunman dressed in military fatigues drove onto the historic Main Square in Kraków, Poland's second-largest city, and opened fire at r Why it matters: European interior ministries are contending with three overlapping pressures at once: domestic political violence, sustained street protests over living costs, and hybrid aviation disruptions that French prosecutors now explicitly suspect of foreign state sponsorship.
► Post-Midterm Fallout in Washington and the Erdoğan-Trump Call Days after Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections — a result The Hill attributed in part to voter opposition to the eight-month Iran war and tariff policies — President Donald Trump called on the Department of Justice to inv Why it matters: An incoming Democratic Congress narrows the White House's domestic room for an open-ended Middle East campaign just as Ankara steps up direct leader-to-leader outreach between Washington and regional capitals.
► Yemen's Front Line Shifts on the Ground While Red Sea Toll Emails Continue Fighting inside Yemen intensified on Saturday as internationally recognized government forces reported ground advances and 875 operations neutralizing 130 Houthi fighters, while Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that coalition airstrikes on t Why it matters: Baghdad's removal of militia-linked firms from Mosul Airport and Yerevan's public pivot toward Ankara show smaller regional states actively reducing their exposure to weakened external patrons.
► Paraguay's Banking Collapse Brings Criminal Charges Against Ex-President Peña Prosecutors in Paraguay filed formal criminal charges against former President Santiago Peña and requested his preventive detention following a systemic banking collapse that toppled his administration and left millions of citizens unable to access t Why it matters: A sovereign banking freeze that removes a sitting president within days sets a stark warning for Latin American financial regulators managing dollar liquidity and domestic bank supervision.
■ The Bottom Line Israel's political deadlock broke toward the opposition on Saturday as President Herzog handed Gadi Eisenkot 28 days and a 67-seat mandate to form a government without Benjamin Netanyahu. In Washington, the political aftermath of Tuesday's midterms is already reshaping foreign policy expectations as President Trump spars with an incoming Democratic Congress while speaking with Turkey's President Erdoğan on Iran and Ukraine. item.title: Strategic Brief: Iran Sets a Two-Day Price for Hormuz, a Qatari LNG Carrier Is Hit in the Gulf, and Trump Says Ukraine Needs a New Leader Two Days Before the US Midterms
item.description:
Istanbul's talks have not yet sat, but Iran has already named its terms for reopening the strait — sanctions relief, US force withdrawals and billions in frozen funds — while the election deadline in Washington is now hours away. Europe's youth protest wave turned violent in Frankfurt, and Bulgaria elected its first female president on a platform of dialogue with Moscow.
► Tehran Puts a Two-Day Number on Hormuz Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that talks with Qatari mediators had produced a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of any agreement with Washington, shortened from an earlier five-day figure. Why it matters: The two-day window is a specific, testable offer for the first time. If it survives Tuesday, Washington faces a clear choice between a visible reopening of the world's most consequential oil chokepoint and a strike package it has already assembled.
► Qatar's Own LNG Carrier Is Hit While Doha Mediates Nakilat, Qatar's state-linked gas transport company, said the LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by 'unidentified objects' on Friday evening in the Gulf. Why it matters: The mediator's own export fleet is now a target. That narrows Qatar's room to keep brokering on purely neutral ground, and it puts a Gulf state's sovereign assets directly on the retaliation list for whichever side is responsible.
► Trump Tells Kyiv to Change Its President, and Kherson's Truce Ends President Trump repeated his call for Ukraine to hold elections and suggested it get a new leader, blaming President Zelensky for a US deal to buy Russian diesel that reversed years of American sanctions on that trade (AP, BBC). Why it matters: Public US pressure on Zelensky's legitimacy, delivered days before a summit track is due to reconvene, undercuts his position at the table. It also tells Moscow that Washington's patience is a variable it can work on while Ukraine's air defences thin out.
► Frankfurt Burns, and Europe's Youth Protest Wave Turns Violent Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as cost-of-living protests turned violent in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg. Why it matters: Both countries are core NATO members now facing domestic resistance tied directly to defence spending and conscription. That is a political constraint on rearmament that will show up in budgets, not just in street clashes.
► Bulgaria Elects Its First Woman President, and She Favours Talking to Moscow Incumbent President Iliana Iotova won Sunday's runoff with between 57. 4 and 58. 2 percent against Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition, on 38. 6 to 39. Why it matters: Bulgaria sits on NATO's Black Sea flank and hosts the alliance's eastern air-policing rotations. A president who opposes arming Ukraine, elected outright, is a durable marker of how far Russian-aligned sentiment still reaches inside the EU's southeastern edge.
► Beijing Makes Routine Patrols the Baseline East of Taiwan Taiwan's Coast Guard said Beijing has no jurisdiction over waters around Taiwan, after China's coast guard claimed a flotilla led by the Hushi conducted 'routine law enforcement patrols' east of the island and said it had stepped up control of the su Why it matters: Coast guard presence creates a legal claim that grey-zone military exercises do not. Beijing is converting periodic pressure into a standing administrative fact on Taiwan's eastern approaches, the side that faces the Pacific and any external reinforcement.
► Gaza: Eight Killed in a Year-Old Ceasefire, and the Peace Plan Stalls Israeli strikes in Gaza killed at least eight people, including a four-year-old boy, despite a ceasefire that took effect in October last year. Why it matters: A ceasefire with a daily kill rate is not a ceasefire, and the stalled peace plan means no mechanism exists to change that....

item.title: Strategic Brief: Zelensky Lands in Istanbul to Map a November Summit, Beijing Expands Coast Guard Patrols East of Taiwan, and Syria Asks About Joining the Makkah Bloc
item.description:
Three of the four tracks that matter this week moved on the same weekend: Ukraine's diplomacy hardened into a concrete trilateral timetable, China began treating Taiwan's eastern approaches as a routine enforcement space, and Damascus opened the door to the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani security pact. In Tehran, diplomacy and a strike package are running in parallel.
► Istanbul, Abu Dhabi or Geneva: Ukraine's Talks Get a Date President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Istanbul on Saturday at President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's invitation, his office confirmed on Telegram, for talks covering Black Sea shipping security, bilateral defence cooperation and the diplomatic track towa Why it matters: A date on a calendar is the first concrete deliverable of the autumn diplomatic push. If the Nov 6-10 window holds, it will be the first trilateral contact since the US posture toward Kyiv shifted, and the Black Sea agenda gives both sides something to trade that is not territory.
► Beijing Calls the Waters East of Taiwan Its Enforcement Zone China's Coast Guard said on Oct 31 that a flotilla led by its Hulishi vessel conducted a 'routine law enforcement patrol' in the waters east of Taiwan, part of what state media described as stepped-up control of the area through October (People's Dai Why it matters: Patrols east of Taiwan test the resupply corridor that any defence of the island depends on, and this weekend's parallel move near Pratas extends the same logic into the South China Sea. It also lands days before APEC's leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov 18-19, giving Beijing a claim of normalcy to defend in the room.
► The Quad Reassembles Around Chokepoints, Not Around China On the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his counterparts from Australia, India and Japan on Saturday — the Quad format — before chairing the closing session on freedom of navigation in the Why it matters: Chokepoint security has become the lowest-common-denominator agenda for the Indo-Pacific grouping, which tells you how much of the region's strategic anxiety is now maritime and economic rather than territorial. It also explains why the Quad could meet productively in the same city where the G20 could not produce a communique at all.
► Atlanta Produced No Communique, and That Was the Plan The G20 foreign ministers' meeting closed on Oct 31 without a joint communique. Why it matters: A G20 that cannot sign a paragraph on Ukraine or Iran while Russia sits at the table has stopped functioning as a crisis-management forum. The Miami summit in December now carries the burden, and the US has pre-committed to a low-ambition format.
► In Tehran, a Two-Day Hormuz Plan Sits Beside a Strike Package Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Sunday that talks are under way with Qatari mediators on a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US accepts Tehran's conditions (Al Jazeera, Nov 1). Why it matters: The gap between a two-day reopening plan and a geographically unrestricted retaliation doctrine is the whole story. Both tracks are live because both sides are using the other as leverage — and the midterm vote on Tuesday is the switch that changes the calculation.
► Damascus Circles a Defence Pact It Cannot Yet Afford to Join Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said on Saturday that 'discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance,' speaking at the IISS Manama Dialogue in Bahrain (Daily Sabah, AFP). Why it matters: A Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani mutual defence bloc adding Syria would extend a Sunni-majority security architecture from the Gulf to the Levant, covering three of the region's live fronts. item.title: Strategic Brief: Russia and the US Veto Each Other's Resolutions and Let MINURSO's Mandate Lapse, as Moscow Stalls Talks in Atlanta and Qatar Drafts a Nuclear Deal for Tehran
item.description:
The Security Council failed to renew the Western Sahara mission after an unprecedented double veto, the first time the MINURSO file has broken down outright. In Atlanta, Lavrov froze the G20, and in Tehran a Qatari-brokered framework has begun to take written shape.
► Western Sahara: the Security Council vetoes itself into an unmonitored ceasefire The Security Council failed on Friday 30 October to renew the mandate of MINURSO, the UN mission that has monitored the Western Sahara ceasefire since 1991. Why it matters: MINURSO is one of the last functioning constraints on a 50-year-old territorial dispute. If the mandate lapses, ceasefire monitoring and mine action in a 266,000 sq km contested territory lose their legal basis, and Polisario and Rabat lose the only third party that verified the line.
► Atlanta: Lavrov arrives, the family photo is cancelled, and the G20 admits it has no consensus At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's presence — at Rubio's own invitation — dominated the two-day session. Why it matters: A G20 that cannot produce a joint communique on two simultaneous wars has stopped functioning as a crisis-management body. The workaround visible here — ad hoc coalitions signing statements outside the consensus process — is how the US is now trying to run economic statecraft, and it is a much weaker instrument than a communique.
► Tehran: a Qatari delegation arrives with a Vance letter and a seven-day draft A Qatari delegation led by a senior adviser to the prime minister and foreign minister arrived in Tehran on Friday morning, coordinating with Washington, according to Iran's state agency IRNA. Why it matters: The draft is the first written structure to emerge in seven months of war, and its seven-day Hormuz trigger is the part that matters economically.
► Hormuz: four tankers burn, and the IRGC says they used 'unauthorised routes' The IRGC said four oil tankers caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz while travelling along what it called unauthorised routes, Al Jazeera reported on Saturday. Why it matters: Traffic through Hormuz is now being policed by the party that closed it: the IRGC is defining which routes are legal and burning ships that use others. That is a de facto licensing regime over roughly a fifth of global oil trade, and it would survive a ceasefire unless the reopening terms in the draft are enforced by someone other than the IRGC.

It also normalises direct Russian-Ukrainian official contact in occupied territory — a small, real shift in how the war might one day be unwound, and one the Kremlin is deliberately keeping small.
► The rest of the board: Patriot interceptors for Kyiv, a defence bank charter, and Aden under missile fire The State Department approved a $2. 1bn sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine on Friday, funded by Canada, Germany, Norway and the EU loan rather than US money. Why it matters: The Patriot sale is the model that has replaced direct US aid to Kyiv: European and allied money, American hardware, no American appropriation. The Aden strikes show the Houthis now hold two capitals under fire at once while their missiles also reach Saudi infrastructure — a single militia sustaining two separate fronts.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Tanker Mined in Hormuz and Houthi Missiles Hit Saudi Refineries, Even After Iran and Riyadh Agreed to Talk
item.description:
Mines in the Strait of Hormuz and a six-target Houthi salvo on Saudi oil and airport infrastructure undercut this week's Tehran diplomacy, while Washington's last diplomatic overture to Iran runs on a seven-day clock that starts only if Tehran freezes its nuclear programme first.
► Hormuz: mines, burning tankers and a strait nobody can reopen Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said three tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after striking naval mines, and that a fourth vessel hit mines in the eastern part of the waterway, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage on Friday Why it matters: A mined Hormuz plus a proposal that hinges on Iran giving up its nuclear leverage before anything is eased are the two poles of this crisis. Nothing that has happened this week moves them closer together.
► Houthis strike Ras Tanura and Riyadh's airport days after Iran-Saudi talks Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on X that the group carried out six operations: a ballistic missile at the Ras Tanura refinery, a missile at an Aramco facility in Abqaiq, multiple missiles at King Khalid International Airpor Why it matters: If Iran cannot or will not stop Houthi strikes during its own diplomatic opening, Riyadh's incentive to bankroll a US-Iran deal weakens sharply. Saudi consent is what makes a Gulf-wide escalation tolerable for Washington.
► Dnipro strike kills 14 as a US-brokered truce holds in Kherson A Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 others, including an 11-year-old boy, according to Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha Why it matters: The same week Washington eased sanctions on Moscow, a Russian drone killed 14 civilians at a Ukrainian station. That contradiction is now the central political problem for Kyiv's supporters — and a humanitarian truce that may double as a Russian resupply window gives them little to show for it.
► The EU offers Canada a status that does not yet exist European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the two-day Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Thursday that 'associate membership' would be 'a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before', open only to the clos Why it matters: A new membership category designed for one country is a small institutional change with a large precedent: it gives the EU a way to bind democratic middle powers closer without treaty change or enlargement votes.
► Washington sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over M23 The US Treasury sanctioned Rwanda's defence ministry and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a bank serving Rwandan security services, over support for the M23 rebellion in eastern DR Congo, the BBC reported. Why it matters: This is the first time Washington has sanctioned a Rwandan government ministry rather than individuals, and it cuts at the bank that pays Kigali's soldiers. It tests whether a US-brokered deal can be enforced on its own signatory — and whether coltan supply chains react.
► The rest of the board: China's purges, Lagarde's exit, a $3bn exchange freeze China's fifth plenum expelled a record 33 Central Committee members, 16 of them from the military, and attendance fell below 300 for the first time in Xi Jinping's 14 years of leadership — 279 members against 315 a year earlier, per the BBC. Why it matters: Three unrelated but telling data points: the largest purge cycle of Xi's tenure hitting the military hardest, the eurozone's chief central banker leaving to speak politically, and the world's biggest crypto venue freezing billions — all in 48 hours.
■ The Bottom Line Iran is publicly describing the Strait of Hormuz as mined while a Qatari-brokered Vance letter asks it to freeze its nuclear programme before the strait reopens — an offer Tehr...

item.title: Strategic Brief: Israel's Election Hands No One a Mandate as Washington Readies a Post-Midterm Strike Package on Iran
item.description:
With 85 percent of Israeli ballots counted, Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 seats and the opposition 48 — no majority for either — while the White House has told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterms, and Brent settles above $115 after a Houthi missile claim against Saudi Arabia's largest refinery.
► Israel Votes: A Fragmented Result and a Military That Refuses to Be Drawn In Partial official results with 85. Why it matters: A caretaker government with no majority is the weakest possible position from which to launch or sustain a new war with Iran.
► Washington Signals a Post-Midterm Offensive; Tehran Says the Mediation Is Not an Offer The Wall Street Journal reported that the US has warned several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a short, intense military offensive against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, though people briefed on the conversations said Trump has not mad Why it matters: Both tracks are running at once — a letter aimed at reviving talks and a warning to Gulf hosts to prepare for war — and neither is close to closing. The sequencing dispute (nuclear first versus sanctions relief first) is the actual deadlock, and the midterms are now the operative deadline for whichever way Washington goes.
► Yemen: Aden Airport Hit Twice, a Saudi Refinery Claimed, Brent Settles at $115 Two ballistic missiles struck the perimeter of Aden airport on Wednesday, wounding civilians and causing damage, according to government forces spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili, who described it as the sixth such attack on the facility. Why it matters: The Houthis have moved from disrupting Red Sea shipping to striking the world's largest crude exporter's most important refinery and the seat of Yemen's recognised government. That is a different war from the one that began in February, and the market is pricing it as such.
► Ukraine: A Local Ceasefire Holds While Russia Hits Bridges and Romania Confronts a Sabotage Network The US-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Kherson Oblast, has held into its second day. Why it matters: The Oleshky truce is a genuine and unusual development — a Russian-requested, First Lady-brokered local ceasefire that expanded in scope — but it is running in parallel with an intensifying campaign against Ukrainian bridges and logistics.
► The First Island Chain Gets a Name and a Doctrine Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met in Cebu on the sidelines of the ASEAN defence meetings and agreed on efforts to 'implement an effective denial defence in the First Island Chain' — the arc running f Why it matters: 'Effective denial defence in the First Island Chain' is a doctrinal commitment to hold the line at the maritime geography rather than defend from behind it, and it now has both governments' names on it.
► Spain: A Rail Disaster and a Political Reckoning Two high-speed trains collided in Toledo province in central Spain, killing at least 68 people and injuring more than 100, according to Euronews and Xinhua. Why it matters: Europe's deadliest rail accident in years lands on a Spanish government already under pressure, and the protest demand for resignations converts a safety failure into a governing crisis.
■ The Bottom Line Today's central fact is that nobody can decide anything: Israel has voted no majority to either bloc, Iran has called the Qatari draft not an offer, and Washington has warned Gulf states to prepare for strikes it says it has not yet ordered. The Oleshky truce is real and held through a second day, but it is a local humanitarian arrangement, not a peace process, and Russia spent the same period putting four Iskander missiles into a Kyiv bridge. Watch three dates: Friday's completion of Israel's count, the November 3 US midterms, and Tehran's promised response to Qat...

item.title: Strategic Brief: Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Russian Su-35s and Signs Up for S-400s as 50,000 Flee Its Southern Borderlands
item.description:
Abiy Ahmed announced the accelerated delivery at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on the same day UNHCR said refugee flows into Kenya had jumped from 36,000 to 50,000 in 24 hours. Israel also voted to a deadlock, and the Gulf opened a direct channel to Tehran that has not yet produced a deal.
► Ethiopia's Russian Arms Package Lands in the Middle of a Spreading War Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets, a year earlier than the existing contract required, and will acquire four S-400 air defence batteries. Why it matters: Russia has just accelerated delivery of front-line combat aircraft and strategic air defence to a government fighting three internal wars and drifting toward conflict with its neighbour. That is a durable Russian foothold on the Red Sea's western flank, at the chokepoint the Gulf war has already made more valuable.
► Israel Votes to a Deadlock, and the Arab Parties Hold the Balance With 85 percent of ballots counted, BBC News reports Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies on track for 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, against 48 for former army chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc. Why it matters: Israel is fighting an eight-month war with Iran and a continuing campaign in the north while its government's composition is unresolved for weeks. Whoever assembles a coalition will define whether Jerusalem escalates or settles — and a caretaker government has less room to make either choice.
► The Gulf Sends Its Defence Ministers to Tehran — and Gets a No Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud travelled to Tehran on Monday with officials from Pakistan and Turkiye — the three signatories of August's Mecca Joint Defence Agreement — plus Qatari mediators, for the first high-level contact Why it matters: The Gulf states are building a security channel that bypasses Washington, at the moment Washington is threatening another round of strikes. Even if it fails, the attempt itself signals that Riyadh and Doha no longer assume American protection is the default.
► A Kherson Ceasefire Holds, and Europe Is Told It Is Not Invited to the Next Round The truce that began on Tuesday to move food and medicine into Russian-occupied Oleshky has been extended across the wider Kherson region, the BBC reports, with no breaches recorded so far. Why it matters: Washington is now brokering directly with Moscow, with the Vatican and a US first lady as the visible intermediaries, while telling European capitals they are spectators. A local truce is not a peace process — but the shape of the table being set is one Europe is not at.
► Canada and the EU Launch an 'Alliance for the Future' Without Washington Mark Carney hosts European Council President Antonio Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Montreal on 29-30 October for the 21st Canada-EU summit, where the two sides are expected to launch an 'Alliance for the Future' covering trad Why it matters: A formal associate-membership track for a G7 economy is a structural change in how the EU projects outward — built explicitly as insulation from the US. It is the clearest institutional response yet to Washington's tariff campaign.
► Britain's Budget: Paying for Rearmament With a Cost-of-Living Patch Chancellor John Healey delivered the first budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister three months ago. Why it matters: Britain is funding rearmament and Ukraine aid while its independent fiscal watchdog projects stagnating living standards. That is the political arithmetic most NATO members will face within two years — and Healey has not yet said where the defence money comes from.
■ The Bottom Line The day's most consequential move came from Moscow, not the Middle East: Ethiopia took delivery of 12 Su-35s a year ahead of schedule with S-400s to follow,...

item.title: Strategic Brief: Serbia's Vucic Concedes to a Student Movement, Algeria Sends Troops Abroad for the First Time Since 1973, and Jordan Bombs Syria's South
item.description:
Three developments reset different maps on the same day: fourteen years of Serbian strongman rule end at the ballot box, Algeria breaks a five-decade ban on foreign deployments to secure energy assets in Niger, and Jordanian jets strike inside Syria without Damascus's consent.
► Serbia: Vucic Concedes After 14 Years Aleksandar Vucic admitted defeat on Sunday night in Serbia's snap parliamentary election, ending fourteen years in power. According to Serbia's election commission, with 97% of polling stations counted, the student-led Student List took 2. Why it matters: Serbia sits at the junction of EU accession, Russian energy dependence and Balkan stability. A government run by inexperienced anti-corruption activists is an unknown quantity for Brussels, Moscow and the region — and Vucic's 105-seat bloc gives him real capacity to obstruct.
► Algeria Breaks a 53-Year Taboo and Deploys to Niger Algeria's parliament approved sending troops to Niger — its first foreign military deployment since it sent forces to Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. Why it matters: Algeria has spent decades refusing to project force abroad, and that posture was a core part of its non-alignment identity.
► Jordan Bombs Southern Syria, and Damascus Denies It Agreed Jordanian aircraft struck targets in southern Syria on Monday in retaliation for Friday's gun attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, which killed at least nine people. Why it matters: Jordan has spent the past year trying to stay out of regional wars. Striking inside Syria is a new posture, and the dispute over whether Damascus consented points to a deeper problem: the Syrian government's inability to control the south, which borders both Jordan and the Israeli-occupied Golan.
► Iran Talks: Tehran Says Washington Is Not Serious, and a Ship Burns off Iraq Iran accused Washington of not being serious about negotiations, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage, as Gulf shipping risks rose again: the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a vessel on fire 63 nautical miles southeast of al-Faw, Iraq Why it matters: The Mecca pact — signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in August, with an attack on one treated as an attack on all — was built as a counterweight to Iran. Its members are now in Tehran negotiating directly with the Iranian security establishment.
► Ukraine: Kyiv Hit Hours Before an Oleshky Truce, and Romania Names a Russian Hand Russian strikes on Kyiv late on Monday killed one person and wounded eight, with mayor Vitali Klitschko reporting damage to medical facilities including an intensive care unit. Why it matters: The Oleshky truce is the first localised ceasefire of this phase of the war, and it began with a mass-casualty strike on the capital. The Brasov finding, plus the shipping attacks, shows the sabotage campaign against NATO's Black Sea flank has moved from deniable to prosecutable.
► Also Watching: Israel Votes Today Under a Hebron Operation, and Merz Goes to Asia Israel holds its general election on Tuesday with the military operation in Hebron still running. Why it matters: An Israeli election held during a mass-displacement operation in Hebron will shape whether the West Bank policy continues or is reversed. Merz's Asia trip and Steinmeier's China visit in the same week signal Berlin hedging its supply chains and security ties away from a single reliance on Washington.
■ The Bottom Line Vucic's loss is the day's biggest change: a student movement born from a train-station disaster now holds 52.7% of the vote and no governing experience, in a country that straddles EU accession and Russian energy. Algeria's vote to send troops to Niger ends a 53-year refusal to deploy abroad, turning a gas-pipeline route into a military commitment in the Sahel. item.title: Strategic Brief: Houthi Missiles Reach Mecca and Medina's Airspace, Kim Jong Un Inaugurates the Yalu Bridge, and Brazil Votes in a Coin-Toss Runoff
item.description:
Iran-aligned Houthis claim strikes on three Saudi airports and Saudi oil sites while Riyadh reports intercepts over Islam's two holiest cities. Kim Jong Un crosses into China for the first time in over a year as Pyongyang's ties with Seoul deteriorate. Brazilians choose between Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

Why it matters: Strikes framed as reaching Mecca and Medina convert a proxy war into a legitimacy crisis for the Saudi leadership, and Aden's fourth airport strike this month shows the Houthis can now hit both the Saudi depth and the Yemeni government's seat simultaneously. Every escalation raises the price of the de-escalation Washington is trying to engineer.
► Tehran and Washington Trade Blame as Trump Floats a Strike 'as Soon as Sunday' President Trump said the US is considering a possible attack on Iran as soon as Sunday, telling reporters Washington might have to 'finish the job' or could instead reach a major deal with Tehran, Al Jazeera's live coverage reported on Sunday. Why it matters: The gap between an imminent strike and a signed deal is now measured in hours, and both principals are campaigning. A decision taken under electoral pressure would set the terms of the next phase of the Gulf war with little room for reversal.
► Kim Jong Un Crosses the Yalu as Pyongyang Leans Toward Beijing Kim Jong Un travelled into China on Saturday, crossing the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge to the border city of Dandong, according to South Korea's unification ministry and China's Xinhua news agency. For Washington and Seoul, it removes any near-term hope of splitting North Korea from China on denuclearisation.

Why it matters: A private company's terms of service now shape the tactical picture on a European battlefield, and the White House and the company disagree publicly about who pulled the lever. The Black Sea numbers show the maritime war escalating in parallel, and both push European capitals toward building alternatives they do not currently have.
► Europe's Streets Stay Full as France Turns to Its Presidential Calendar France's interior ministry put Saturday's nationwide turnout at 410,000, including 110,000 in Paris, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000, the Associated Press reported. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests. Why it matters: The unrest is no longer a single-issue French story but an electoral one: it feeds the National Rally ahead of the May presidential vote and is echoed in Italy and Albania. Bulgaria's vote adds a Black Sea security dimension to an otherwise ceremonial office.
► Brazil's Coin-Toss Runoff, and a Tariff Trimmed for Maine Brazil votes on Sunday in a presidential runoff between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of the former president jailed for plotting a coup after the 2022 election. Why it matters: A Brazilian result either way will not settle the country's polarisation, and the size of the Lula rally suggests the runoff will be close enough to be contested. The Canadian tariff adjustment is a small but telling case of trade policy being tuned to individual Senate races weeks before an election.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Beijing's $14bn Taiwan Arms Package Stalls as Trump Courts Xi, While the Kremlin Calls the Ukraine Peace Draft Thin and France Bans Saturday Protests
item.description:
Taiwan has waited months for Washington to clear a $14 billion package of Patriots, command systems and a 360-degree radar for its T-Dome air defence, and US officials now say the sale is likely to be split into smaller tranches to protect the trade truce with Xi Jinping. Separately, the Kremlin dismissed the latest Ukraine proposals as lacking substance even as it agreed in principle to three-way talks in mid-November, and Paris moved to ban unauthorised demonstrations ahead of a second weekend of unrest.
► Taiwan's Air Defence Package Is Stuck Behind the US-China Truce AFP reported on Friday that Taiwan has been waiting months for President Donald Trump to approve a $14 billion sale of US weapons and equipment. Why it matters: The Taiwan arms pipeline is now being priced by Washington as trade leverage rather than deterrence. Every month of delay moves delivery and training further out, and the option of splitting the package into tranches would let the White House sell the same deterrent twice while Beijing watches.
► The Kremlin Calls the Ukraine Draft Thin, Then Agrees to Talk in November Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday that Russia was in principle ready to resume trilateral talks in mid-November, after the US midterm elections, and that Moscow wanted them t Why it matters: Moscow has agreed to a date without agreeing to terms, and it set the date after the US midterms. That sequencing gives Russia leverage over what Washington puts on the table, while Ukraine's two most sensitive dependencies — Starlink and Patriot-class interceptors — are both being rationed by Washington and its contractors.
► France Bans Protests and Extends Curfews Before a Second Weekend President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that illegitimate protests would be banned in the coming days, after meeting intelligence chiefs and senior ministers at the Elysée, RFI reported. Why it matters: A G7 state is governing a cost-of-living protest wave with curfews, protest bans and mass fast-track prosecutions. The trigger is prices — the same energy shock now pushing Brent above $113 — so the political damage in Europe is being imported from the Gulf.
► Oil Settles Above $113 as the Gulf Risk Premium Outlives the Hormuz Recovery ICE Brent settled 4% higher at just above $113 a barrel on Thursday, its highest since May 4, and was trading at $112. 96 in early Asian hours on Friday; WTI was near $98-99 after a 2. 4% jump, Arab News and CNBC-TV18 reported. Why it matters: The premium in futures is now a bet on what happens after the US midterms, not on today's flows. European gas tells the same story: TTF settled above EUR90/MWh, its highest since December 2022, with EU storage peaking just under 75% — a thin buffer going into winter if Gulf LNG does not return.
► Sudan Denies the Abyei Market Strike as Both Sides Demand an Investigation Sudan's foreign ministry said on Thursday that the Sudanese Armed Forces had absolutely no connection to the October 19 drone attack on Amiet Common Market in Abyei, a trading centre serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities, Radio Tamazuj rep Why it matters: Abyei is the seam between two states and a UN-mandated demilitarised zone, and a mass-casualty drone strike there has now produced competing war-crimes filings rather than a joint inquiry.
► Putin Reshuffles His Government as Washington Talks to Moscow Vladimir Putin signed decrees on Thursday appointing four deputy prime ministers, a new transport minister and a presidential aide, all effective on signing, Xinhua reported. Why it matters: Personnel changes are one of the few reliable signals of what a Kremlin expects to need. Elevating finance and transport officials while the US offers talks suggests Moscow is preparing for a long war economy and a rebuilt logistics chain, ...

item.title: Strategic Brief: Sudanese Army Drones Kill Over 300 in Kordofan and Abyei as South Sudan Lodges a Formal Protest, Britain Sends Fighters to Saudi Arabia, and Japan Puts a 1,000km Missile on Yonaguni
item.description:
A three-day wave of Sudanese army drone strikes has killed more than 300 people, including 153 in the disputed Abyei market, pushing Khartoum and Juba into open confrontation. Britain is now flying defensive combat air patrols over Saudi cities, and Japan has deployed its first long-range land-to-ship missile to the island 110km from Taiwan.
► Sudan's Drone War Crosses Into Abyei Sudanese army drone strikes over the weekend and Monday killed more than 300 people across West Kordofan and the disputed Abyei region, according to reporting by BBC Verify and DW. Why it matters: The war has jumped from an internal army-RSF fight into a Sudan-South Sudan flashpoint over an oil-bearing territory, with UN peacekeepers unable to prevent drone strikes. A border war there would compound the world's largest displacement crisis and put the region's oil infrastructure at risk.
► Britain Flies Its Fighters Over Saudi Cities Britain will run defensive counter-air missions over Saudi Arabia using RAF Typhoon fighters, Downing Street and the Ministry of Defence announced on Tuesday, following a Saudi request after renewed Houthi attacks. Why it matters: A European air force is now committed to defending the world's largest oil exporter's cities and infrastructure. That raises the cost of Houthi escalation, but also the chance of a British casualty or engagement that pulls London deeper in.
► Iran Hardens: No Talks, and a Third Tanker on a Mine Iran's position hardened on two fronts on Tuesday. Why it matters: Diplomacy is stalled on Iran's terms, shipping losses are accumulating, and oil is holding near $110. Iraq closing its Iranian border signals that even Tehran's neighbours are now hedging against it.
► Keen Sword 27: A 1,000km Missile 110km From Taiwan Japan and the United States began Keen Sword 27 on Monday, one of their largest joint exercises, with about 45,000 Japanese troops and 12,000 US personnel, running through next Thursday. Why it matters: Anti-ship missiles able to reach the Chinese mainland are now physically based on the island closest to Taiwan, with European navies participating for the first time. That is a real change in the pre-positioned force posture, not a symbolic exercise.
► Witkoff to Moscow as Washington Squeezes Kyiv US special envoy Steve Witkoff travels to Russia on Wednesday to meet Vladimir Putin, after what a US official called 'constructive' talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo that also involved the Norwegian and Finnish leaders and European and Why it matters: The sequencing — Zelensky in Oslo, then Witkoff in Moscow the next day — suggests Washington is assembling a framework and handing it to the Kremlin. Kyiv is being asked to accept guarantees it cannot verify while its battlefield communications are reportedly being throttled.
■ The Bottom Line Three of today's developments share a pattern: air and drone power is doing the work that ground forces cannot. Sudan's army used drones to kill 300-plus people and drew South Sudan into the war; the Houthis used them to bring Britain into Saudi air defence; Iran used mines and drones to hold Hormuz shut at $110 oil. Japan's answer is pre-positioned missiles on Yonaguni. The diplomatic track is alive but narrow — Witkoff meets Putin Wednesday, and Iran says it will not talk until its conditions are met.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Saudi Arabia Postpones Its Flagship Investment Summit as Egypt Balances Houthi Attacks With a $5.3bn Saudi Deposit, and Japan Puts Coastal Missiles on Yonaguni
item.description:
Riyadh cancelled the 2026 'Davos in the Desert' and told government staff to work from home under repeated Houthi strikes, while Cairo's parliament pushed its vote on sending troops to Saudi Arabia to October 26. In the East China Sea, US and Japanese forces began drills on Yonaguni, 110km from Taiwan, fielding the NMESIS coastal anti-ship system.
► Riyadh Postpones FII as Houthi Strikes Reach the Capital's Everyday Life Saudi Arabia has postponed its Future Investment Initiative until next year, according to a statement on the conference website cited by Al Jazeera (AFP/Reuters). The tenth edition had been scheduled for October 26-29 in Riyadh. Why it matters: The FII is the main annual showcase for Vision 2030 investment. Postponing it, plus remote-work orders in the capital, signals that Riyadh expects the threat to persist for weeks rather than days — and that foreign executives are now part of the risk calculation.
► Egypt's Parliament Stalls the Vote on Sending Forces to Saudi Arabia Egypt's House of Representatives adjourned its vote on authorising military support for Saudi Arabia to October 26, Al Jazeera reported (AFP/Reuters). Why it matters: Cairo is being asked to convert a financial lifeline into a military commitment. The delay shows the el-Sisi government wants procedural cover — and that the Houthi campaign is now pulling in Arab armies beyond the Yemeni battlefield.
► US and Japan Put Missiles on Yonaguni as Drills Begin The US and Japan began joint exercises on Monday that bring advanced missile systems to Yonaguni, the westernmost inhabited island of the Ryukyu chain about 110km from Taiwan, Nikkei Asia reported. Why it matters: This is a permanent-feeling shift in force posture, not a headline exercise. A US anti-ship battery on Yonaguni shortens the distance between Taiwan and allied strike systems, and Beijing will read it as a direct change to the military balance around the island.
► Kiev Says Washington Is Holding Up Missiles Europe Already Paid For President Volodymyr Zelensky told US senators on Monday that the Pentagon is delaying deliveries of air-defence missiles already funded by Ukraine's European allies, Deutsche Welle reported. Why it matters: The argument is no longer about whether the US will fund Ukraine's air defence — Europe is paying — but whether Washington will let the weapons move. If a signature, not money, is the bottleneck, allied procurement becomes a lever the White House can pull at will, and Kyiv's winter air defence depends on US politics.
► Sudan's Drone War Kills Over 160 in Days, and Ethiopia's Tigray Gets an Interim Authority Medics and rights groups say drone attacks across Sudan have killed more than 160 people since Friday, Al Jazeera reported. Why it matters: Sudan's war is now being decided by cheap drones striking markets and displacement camps — a pattern with no front line to negotiate over, which makes mediation harder. In Ethiopia, a Tigray settlement that leaves the Eritrea question open keeps a second war risk alive in the same region.
► Iran and Germany Trade Ambassadors, and the Houthis Hit Yemen's Army Iran's foreign ministry summoned Germany's ambassador Axel Dittmann on Monday, Arab News reported, after Berlin summoned Iran's ambassador over an alleged plot to assassinate pro-Israel figures. Why it matters: Europe is now prosecuting Iran-linked plots in its own courts, which turns the Iran war into a European domestic security matter. And with Brent above $110, the Houthi campaign is being priced into global energy costs, not just Gulf security.
■ The Bottom Line Riyadh's decision to postpone its flagship investment summit and move the capital's government offices to remote work shows the Houthi campaign has crossed from a military problem into an economic one. Egypt's delayed vote indicates Arab partners will move slowly and with condition...

item.title: Strategic Brief: Ukraine Fires 1,015 Drones at Russia as Trump Attacks the Strikes, Taipei Repels 16 Chinese Vessels, and France Counts 2,400 Arrests
item.description:
Ukraine's largest drone campaign of the war hit St Petersburg's oil terminal and closed its airport overnight; Washington responded by attacking Kyiv rather than Moscow. Taiwan's coast guard pushed back a coordinated Chinese flotilla near Dongsha, and Macron addressed the nation after riots gutted a city hall in Limoges.
► Kyiv Sends 1,015 Drones Into Russia Overnight Russia's Defence Ministry said it neutralised 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight across 15 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea, Al Jazeera reports — one of Kyiv's largest aerial operations of the war. Why it matters: The US is now simultaneously blocking new sanctions and criticising the only coercive tool Kyiv still has. Watch whether Congress moves to override the 60-day waiver or whether allied refinery supplies to Ukraine become the substitute.
► Taipei Drives Off 16 Chinese Vessels in a Coordinated Sweep Taiwan's coast guard said on Sunday it confronted and drove away 16 Chinese coast guard, research and fishing vessels taking part in what it called simultaneous 'maritime harassment' operations around Taiwan's main island and Pratas (Dongsha), the di Why it matters: Beijing is normalising jurisdiction-by-presence around Taiwan and Dongsha without firing a shot. Every encounter that Taipei resolves with water cannon and eviction establishes the operating procedure for the next, larger one.
► France's Cost-of-Living Revolt Turns Into the Worst Disorder in Decades Some 550,000 demonstrators marched across France on Saturday over fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services including schools. Why it matters: Macron's room to sell defence spending, Ukraine aid and EU fiscal reform to voters shrinks with every torched building. French political weakness directly weakens the EU's ability to act on Ukraine and trade.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Trump Says Washington Is in Denuclearisation Talks With Russia and China After New START's Lapse, as Wang Yi Tells Israel to Reverse West Bank Settlements

Trump confirmed on Newsmax that the US is negotiating nuclear disarmament with Moscow and Beijing weeks after the last US-Russia arms treaty expired, while China's foreign minister used a summit in Baku to call the Palestinian question 'the greatest historical injustice of this century' and demand Israel stop expanding settlements.

Why it matters: With New START gone, there is now no treaty cap on the two largest arsenals. Trump's claim of trilateral talks is unverified and likely aspirational - China has repeatedly refused to join a US-Russia framework - but the statement itself is a signal that arms control has moved from a structured treaty regime to ad hoc leader-level diplomacy.

Kyiv's $79bn ask - and Europe's hesitation over how to fund it - will determine whether Ukraine can hold its energy grid and front line through the winter without US backing.

Why it matters: The ceasefire that was meant to let aid in is not preventing famine-level outcomes, and the commercial-supply halt removes the market component that keeps prices in check. With winter approaching and aid groups unable to meet needs alone, the humanitarian trajectory is worsening even under a nominal truce.

Combined with the unresolved Ethiopia-Eritrea standoff, the Horn remains a live conflict zone where a wider regional war could still break out.

item.title: Strategic Brief: US Weighs Its Largest Non-Nuclear Bomb for Iran as Trump Rules Out Ground Troops, and Kyiv Breaks Openly With Washington Over Starshield and Russian Refineries
item.description:
The Pentagon has drawn up strike options that include the GBU-43 'mother of all bombs' even as Trump insists no US ground troops will enter Iran, while Ukraine abandons Trump's no-strike pledge on Russian oil after a White House-ordered cut to its Starshield satellite link.

Why it matters: A publicized option to use the largest conventional bomb signals that Washington is preparing for hardened, deeply buried targets in Iran, not a winding-down. But pairing it with an explicit no-ground-troops pledge shows Trump wants escalation options that do not put Americans in combat - a narrow, fragile line.
► Ukraine Breaks the No-Strike Deal as a White House Order Cuts Its Satellite Link President Zelensky said on Oct 15 that Kyiv would no longer abide by Trump's demand not to strike Russian oil refineries, and Ukrainian drones hit a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight, according to Reuters. Why it matters: This is the sharpest US-Ukraine rupture of the war: an ally's critical military link apparently throttled by the White House, and Kyiv retaliating by striking the Russian oil infrastructure Washington wanted spared. Whoever ordered the Starshield slowdown handed Moscow a battlefield advantage and pushed Europe to hedge against US reliability.
► Houthi Missiles Hit Yemen's Presidential Palace in Aden Houthi forces fired five missiles at the Al-Ma'ashiq presidential palace compound in Aden on Oct 15, killing at least five people, including security guards and civilian employees, and wounding 16, according to Yemen's government and Reuters. Why it matters: Striking the government's own seat in Aden, not just Saudi territory, shows the Houthis can reach the coalition's political core and are deliberately tying the Yemen war to the Iran blockade. It raises the odds Riyadh escalates directly into Yemen.

The hybrid-car cap shows Brussels is willing to use trade tools, but the summit's splits suggest funding both rearmament and industrial protection will be hard.

Rising red ballots against the frontrunner show the race is still open and veto politics are hardening.

item.title: Strategic Brief: China Sails the Liaoning Through the Ryukyus as Asian Stocks Slide on a Hot US Inflation Print, and a Tanker Burns in Romanian Waters
item.description:
Beijing sent its carrier Liaoning through the gap between Okinawa and Miyako and launched fighters 250km south of Ishigaki ahead of expanded US-Japan drills, while hotter-than-expected US inflation triggered the worst global equity selloff in months — the Kospi down 7.6% — and a tanker caught fire in Romania as Black Sea drone attacks spread.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Saudi Coalition Bombs Sanaa's Fuel Depot as the Houthis Vow a 'Painful' Reply, and Russia Hits Kyiv's Power Grid With No Allied Warning

item.title: Strategic Brief: Ethiopia Retakes Adigrat as Its War With Eritrea Escalates, Sudan Buries 72 Miners Killed on the Egyptian Border, and Pakistan Jails Hundreds Under Emergency Rule
item.description:
While attention stays fixed on Riyadh and the Gulf, two interstate wars and a democracy crackdown in South Asia moved sharply forward — a Horn of Africa conflict drawing in drones and foreign patrons, a strike on Sudanese gold miners that kills 72, and Pakistan's army-backed suspension of an entire provincial government.

Continued disruption keeps energy and freight prices high and narrows the space for any negotiated reopening.

Meanwhile the Ukraine war continues with mass-casualty strikes on civilian housing, showing the energy-ceasefire talk has not translated into reduced violence on the ground.

item.title: Strategic Brief: Washington Sanctions the Entire ICC Hours After a Former Court Judge Wins the Nobel Peace Prize, as the Houthis Kill 12 at Riyadh's Airport and Trump Weighs Joining the Yemen War

Taiwan's munitions top-up shows Taipei reading the blockade risk as real and imminent rather than theoretical, while China's reluctance to spend big suggests it is preserving fiscal room for a longer confrontation.

Why it matters: Washington is converting a sanctions-and-arrest campaign into direct control over Venezuelan crude — extending the logic of US energy leverage from the Gulf to the Western Hemisphere.

It also keeps the Gaza file — and the ICC warrants that triggered Friday's sanctions — as a permanent fault line in Western politics.
